segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: … The Last Question …
segments.delivery: Announce the chapter title clearly, with a brief pause before and after.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
By Isaac Asimov

Isaac Asimov was the most prolific science fiction author of all time. In fifty years he averaged a new magazine article, short story, or book every two weeks, and most of that on a manual typewriter. Asimov thought that *The Last Question*, first copyrighted in 1956, was his best short story ever. Even if you do not have the background in science to be familiar with all of the concepts presented here, the ending packs more impact than any other book that I've ever read. Don't read the end of the story first!

> *This is by far my favorite story of all those I have written.
> 
>      After all, I undertook to tell several trillion years of human history in the space of a short story and I leave it to you as to how well I succeeded. I also undertook another task, but I won't tell you what that was lest l spoil the story for you.
> 
>      It is a curious fact that innumerable readers have asked me if I wrote this story. They seem never to remember the title of the story or (for sure) the author, except for the vague thought it might be me. But, of course, they never forget the story itself especially the ending. The idea seems to drown out everything -- and I'm satisfied that it should.*

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
The last question was asked for the first time, half in jest, on May 21, 2061, at a time when humanity first stepped into the light. The question came about as a result of a five-dollar bet over highballs, and it happened this way:

Alexander Adell and Bertram Lupov were two of the faithful attendants of Multivac. As well as any human beings could, they knew what lay behind the cold, clicking, flashing face -- miles and miles of face -- of that giant computer. They had at least a vague notion of the general plan of relays and circuits that had long since grown past the point where any single human could possibly have a firm grasp of the whole.

Multivac was self-adjusting and self-correcting. It had to be, for nothing human could adjust and correct it quickly enough or even adequately enough. So Adell and Lupov attended the monstrous giant only lightly and superficially, yet as well as any men could. They fed it data, adjusted questions to its needs and translated the answers that were issued. Certainly they, and all others like them, were fully entitled to share in the glory that was Multivac's.

For decades, Multivac had helped design the ships and plot the trajectories that enabled man to reach the Moon, Mars, and Venus, but past that, Earth's poor resources could not support the ships. Too much energy was needed for the long trips. Earth exploited its coal and uranium with increasing efficiency, but there was only so much of both.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
But slowly Multivac learned enough to answer deeper questions more fundamentally, and on May 14, 2061, what had been theory, became fact.

The energy of the sun was stored, converted, and utilized directly on a planet-wide scale. All Earth turned off its burning coal, its fissioning uranium, and flipped the switch that connected all of it to a small station, one mile in diameter, circling the Earth at half the distance of the Moon. All Earth ran by invisible beams of sunpower.

Seven days had not sufficed to dim the glory of it and Adell and Lupov finally managed to escape from the public functions, and to meet in quiet where no one would think of looking for them, in the deserted underground chambers, where portions of the mighty buried body of Multivac showed. Unattended, idling, sorting data with contented lazy clickings, Multivac, too, had earned its vacation and the boys appreciated that. They had no intention, originally, of disturbing it.

They had brought a bottle with them, and their only concern at the moment was to relax in the company of each other and the bottle.

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "It's amazing when you think of it,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Adell. His broad face had lines of weariness in it, and he stirred his drink slowly with a glass rod, watching the cubes of ice slur clumsily about.

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "All the energy we can possibly ever use for free. Enough energy, if we wanted to draw on it, to melt all Earth into a big drop of impure liquid iron, and still never miss the energy so used. All the energy we could ever use, forever and forever and forever."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Lupov cocked his head sideways. He had a trick of doing that when he wanted to be contrary, and he wanted to be contrary now, partly because he had had to carry the ice and glassware.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Not forever,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said.

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Oh, hell, just about forever. Till the sun runs down, Bert."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "That's not forever."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "All right, then. Billions and billions of years. Ten billion, maybe. Are you satisfied?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Lupov put his fingers through his thinning hair as though to reassure himself that some was still left and sipped gently at his own drink.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Ten billion years isn't forever."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Well, it will last our time, won't it?"

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "So would the coal and uranium."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "All right, but now we can hook up each individual spaceship to the Solar Station, and it can go to Pluto and back a million times without ever worrying about fuel. You can't do *that* on coal and uranium. Ask Multivac, if you don't believe me.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "I don't have to ask Multivac. I know that."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Then stop running down what Multivac's done for us,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Adell, blazing up,

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "It did all right."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Who says it didn't? What I say is that a sun won't last forever. That's all I'm saying. We're safe for ten billion years, but then what?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Lupov pointed a slightly shaky finger at the other.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "And don't say we'll switch to another sun."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
There was silence for a while. Adell put his glass to his lips only occasionally, and Lupov's eyes slowly closed. They rested.

Then Lupov's eyes snapped open.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "You're thinking we'll switch to another sun when ours is done, aren't you?"

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "I'm not thinking."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Sure you are. You're weak on logic, that's the trouble with you. You're like the guy in the story who was caught in a sudden shower and who ran to a grove of trees and got under one. He wasn't worried, you see, because he figured when one tree got wet through, he would just get under another one."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "I get it,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Adell.

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Don't shout. When the sun is done, the other stars will be gone, too."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Darn right they will,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: muttered Lupov.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "It all had a beginning in the original cosmic explosion, whatever that was, and it'll all have an end when all the stars run down. Some run down faster than others. Hell, the giants won't last a hundred million years. The sun will last ten billion years and maybe the dwarfs will last two hundred billion for all the good they are. But just give us a trillion years and everything will be dark. Entropy has to increase to maximum, that's all."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "I know all about entropy,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Adell, standing on his dignity.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "The hell you do."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "I know as much as you do."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Then you know everything's got to run down someday."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "All right. Who says they won't?"

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "You did, you poor sap. You said we had all the energy we needed, forever. You said 'forever.'

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was Adell's turn to be contrary.

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Maybe we can build things up again someday,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Never."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Why not? Someday."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "Never."

segments.speaker: Alexander Adell
segments.text: "Ask Multivac."

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "*You* ask Multivac. I dare you. Five dollars says it can't be done."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Adell was just drunk enough to try, just sober enough to be able to phrase the necessary symbols and operations into a question which, in words, might have corresponded to this: Will mankind one day without the net expenditure of energy be able to restore the sun to its full youthfulness even after it had died of old age?

Or maybe it could be put more simply like this: How can the net amount of entropy of the universe be massively decreased?

Multivac fell dead and silent. The slow flashing of lights ceased, the distant sounds of clicking relays ended.

Then, just as the frightened technicians felt they could hold their breath no longer, there was a sudden springing to life of the teletype attached to that portion of Multivac. Five words were printed: INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR MEANINGFUL ANSWER.

segments.speaker: Bertram Lupov
segments.text: "No bet,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
whispered Lupov. They left hurriedly.

By next morning, the two, plagued with throbbing head and cottony mouth, had forgotten the incident.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jerrodd, Jerrodine, and Jerrodette I and II watched the starry picture in the visiplate change as the passage through hyperspace was completed in its non-time lapse. At once, the even powdering of stars gave way to the predominance of a single bright shining disk, the size of a marble, centered on the viewing-screen.

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "That's X-23,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
said Jerrodd confidently. His thin hands clamped tightly behind his back and the knuckles whitened.

The little Jerrodettes, both girls, had experienced the hyperspace passage for the first time in their lives and were self-conscious over the momentary sensation of insideoutness. They buried their giggles and chased one another wildly about their mother, screaming,

segments.speaker: Jerrodette I
segments.text: "We've reached X-23 -- we've reached X-23 -- we've --"

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "Quiet, children."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Jerrodine sharply.

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "Are you sure, Jerrodd?"

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "What is there to be but sure?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
asked Jerrodd, glancing up at the bulge of featureless metal just under the ceiling. It ran the length of the room, disappearing through the wall at either end. It was as long as the ship.

Jerrodd scarcely knew a thing about the thick rod of metal except that it was called a Microvac, that one asked it questions if one wished; that if one did not it still had its task of guiding the ship to a preordered destination; of feeding on energies from the various Sub-galactic Power Stations; of computing the equations for the hyperspatial jumps.

Jerrodd and his family had only to wait and live in the comfortable residence quarters of the ship. Someone had once told Jerrodd that the "ac" at the end of "Microvac" stood for ''automatic computer" in ancient English, but he was on the edge of forgetting even that.

Jerrodine's eyes were moist as she watched the visiplate.

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "I can't help it. I feel funny about leaving Earth."

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "Why, for Pete's sake?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: demanded Jerrodd.

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "We had nothing there. We'll have everything on X-23. You won't be alone. You won't be a pioneer. There are over a million people on the planet already. Good Lord, our great-grandchildren will be looking for new worlds because X-23 will be overcrowded."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, after a reflective pause,

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "I tell you, it's a lucky thing the computers worked out interstellar travel the way the race is growing."

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "I know, I know,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
said Jerrodine miserably.

Jerrodette I said promptly,

segments.speaker: Jerrodette I
segments.text: "Our Microvac is the best Microvac in the world."

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "I think so, too,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
said Jerrodd, tousling her hair.

It was a nice feeling to have a Microvac of your own and Jerrodd was glad he was part of his generation and no other. In his father's youth, the only computers had been tremendous machines taking up a hundred square miles of land. There was only one to a planet. Planetary ACs they were called. They had been growing in size steadily for a thousand years and then, all at once, came refinement. In place of transistors, had come molecular valves so that even the largest Planetary AC could be put into a space only half the volume of a spaceship.

Jerrodd felt uplifted, as he always did when he thought that his own personal Microvac was many times more complicated than the ancient and primitive Multivac that had first tamed the Sun, and almost as complicated as Earth's Planetarv AC (the largest) that had first solved the problem of hyperspatial travel and had made trips to the stars possible.

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "So many stars, so many planets,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: sighed Jerrodine, busy with her own thoughts.

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "I suppose families will be going out to new planets forever, the way we are now."

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "Not forever,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Jerrodd, with a smile.

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "It will all stop someday, but not for billions of years. Many billions. Even the stars run down, you know. Entropy must increase.

segments.speaker: Jerrodette II
segments.text: "What's entropy, daddy?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: shrilled Jerrodette II.

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "Entropy, little sweet, is just a word which means the amount of running-down of the universe. Everything runs down, you know, like your little walkie-talkie robot, remember?"

segments.speaker: Jerrodette II
segments.text: "Can't you just put in a new power-unit, like with my robot?"

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "The stars are the power-units. dear. Once they're gone, there are no more power-units."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jerrodette I at once set up a howl.

segments.speaker: Jerrodette I
segments.text: "Don't let them, daddy. Don't let the stars run down."

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "Now look what you've done,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whispered Jerrodine, exasperated.

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "How was I to know it would frighten them?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jerrodd whispered back,

segments.speaker: Jerrodette I
segments.text: "Ask the Microvac,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: wailed Jerrodette I.

segments.speaker: Jerrodette I
segments.text: "Ask him how to turn the stars on again."

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "Go ahead,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Jerrodine.

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "It will quiet them down."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
(Jerrodette II was beginning to cry, also.)

Jerrodd shrugged.

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "Now, now, honeys. I'll ask Microvac. Don't worry, he'll tell us."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He asked the Microvac, adding quickly,

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "Print the answer."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jerrodd cupped the strip or thin cellufilm and said cheerfully,

segments.speaker: Jerrodd
segments.text: "See now, the Microvac says it will take care of everything when the time comes so don't worry."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jerrodine said,

segments.speaker: Jerrodine
segments.text: "And now, children, it's time for bed. We'll be in our new home soon."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Jerrodd read the words on the cellufilm again before destroying it: INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR MEANINGFUL ANSWER.

He shrugged and looked at the visiplate. X-23 was just ahead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: VJ-23X of Lameth stared into the black depths of the three-dimensional, small-scale map of the Galaxy and said,

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Are we ridiculous, I wonder in being so concerned about the matter?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: MQ-17J of Nicron shook his head.

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "I think not. You know the Galaxy will be filled in five years at the present rate of expansion."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Both seemed in their early twenties, both were tall and perfectly formed.

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Still,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said VJ-23X,

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "I hesitate to submit a pessimistic report to the Galactic Council."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "I wouldn't consider any other kind of report. Stir them up a bit. We've got to stir them up."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: VJ-23X sighed.

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Space is infinite. A hundred billion Galaxies are there for the taking. More."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "A hundred billion is not infinite and it's getting less infinite all the time. Consider! Twenty thousand years ago, mankind first solved the problem of utilizing stellar energy, and a few centuries later, interstellar travel became possible. It took mankind a million years to fill one small world and then only fifteen thousand years to fill the rest of the Galaxy. Now the population doubles every ten years --

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: VJ-23X interrupted.

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "We can thank immortality for that."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Very well. Immortality exists and we have to take it into account. I admit it has its seamy side, this immortality. The Galactic AC has solved many problems for us, but in solving the problem of preventing old age and death, it has undone all its other solutions."

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Yet you wouldn't want to abandon life, I suppose."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Not at all,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: snapped MQ-17J, softening it at once to,

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Not yet. I'm by no means old enough. How old are you?"

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Two hundred twenty-three. And you?"

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "I'm still under two hundred. --But to get back to my point. Population doubles every ten years. Once this Galaxy is filled, we'll have filled another in ten years. Another ten years and we'll have filled two more. Another decade, four more. In a hundred years, we'll have filled a thousand Galaxies. In a thousand years, a million Galaxies. In ten thousand years, the entire known universe. Then what?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: VJ-23X said,

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "As a side issue, there's a problem of transportation. I wonder how many sunpower units it will take to move Galaxies of individuals from one Galaxy to the next."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "A very good point. Already, mankind consumes two sunpower units per year."

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Most of it's wasted. After all, our own Galaxy alone pours out a thousand sunpower units a year and we only use two of those."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Granted, but even with a hundred per cent efficiency, we only stave off the end. Our energy requirements are going up in a geometric progression even faster than our population. We'll run out of energy even sooner than we run out of Galaxies. A good point. A very good point."

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "We'll just have to build new stars out of interstellar gas."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Or out of dissipated heat?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: asked MQ-17J, sarcastically.

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "There may be some way to reverse entropy. We ought to ask the Galactic AC."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: VJ-23X was not really serious, but MQ-17J pulled out his AC-contact from his pocket and placed it on the table before him.

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "I've half a mind to,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said.

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "It's something the human race will have to face someday."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
He stared somberly at his small AC-contact. It was only two inches cubed and nothing in itself, but it was connected through hyperspace with the great Galactic AC that served all mankind. Hyperspace considered, it was an integral part of the Galactic AC.

MQ-17J paused to wonder if someday in his immortal life he would get to see the Galactic AC. It was on a little world of its own, a spider webbing of force-beams holding the matter within which surges of submesons took the place of the old clumsy molecular valves. Yet despite its sub-etheric workings, the Galactic AC was known to be a full thousand feet across.

MQ-17J asked suddenly of his AC-contact,

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Can entropy ever be reversed?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: VJ-23X looked startled and said at once,

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "Oh, say, I didn't really mean to have you ask that."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Why not?"

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "We both know entropy can't be reversed. You can't turn smoke and ash back into a tree."

segments.speaker: MQ-17J of Nicron
segments.text: "Do you have trees on your world?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
asked MQ-17J.

The sound of the Galactic AC startled them into silence. Its voice came thin and beautiful out of the small AC-contact on the desk. It said: THERE IS INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR A MEANINGFUL ANSWER.

VJ-23X said,

segments.speaker: VJ-23X of Lameth
segments.text: "See!"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The two men thereupon returned to the question of the report they were to make to the Galactic Council.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Zee Prime's mind spanned the new Galaxy with a faint interest in the countless twists of stars that powdered it. He had never seen this one before. Would he ever see them all? So many of them, each with its load of humanity. --But a load that was almost a dead weight. More and more, the real essence of men was to be found out here, in space.

Minds, not bodies! The immortal bodies remained back on the planets, in suspension over the eons. Sometimes they roused for material activity but that was growing rarer. Few new individuals were coming into existence to join the incredibly mighty throng, but what matter? There was little room in the Universe for new individuals.

Zee Prime was roused out of his reverie upon coming across the wispy tendrils of another mind.

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "I am Zee Prime,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Zee Prime.

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "And you?"

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "I am Dee Sub Wun. Your Galaxy?"

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "We call it only the Galaxy. And you?"

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "We call ours the same. All men call their Galaxy their Galaxy and nothing more. Why not?"

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "True. Since all Galaxies are the same."

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "Not all Galaxies. On one particular Galaxy the race of man must have originated. That makes it different."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Zee Prime said,

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "On which one?"

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "I cannot say. The Universal AC would know."

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "Shall we ask him? I am suddenly curious."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Zee Prime's perceptions broadened until the Galaxies themselves shrank and became a new, more diffuse powdering on a much larger background. So many hundreds of billions of them, all with their immortal beings, all carrying their load of intelligences with minds that drifted freely through space. And yet one of them was unique among them all in being the original Galaxy. One of them had, in its vague and distant past, a period when it was the only Galaxy populated by man.

Zee Prime was consumed with curiosity to see this Galaxy and he called out:

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "Universal AC! On which Galaxy did mankind originate?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
The Universal AC heard, for on every world and throughout space, it had its receptors ready, and each receptor led through hyperspace to some unknown point where the Universal AC kept itself aloof.

Zee Prime knew of only one man whose thoughts had penetrated within sensing distance of Universal AC, and he reported only a shining globe, two feet across, difficult to see.

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "But how can that be all of Universal AC?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Zee Prime had asked.

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Most of it,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: had been the answer,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "is in hyperspace. In what form it is there I cannot imagine."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Nor could anyone, for the day had long since passed, Zee Prime knew, when any man had any part of the making of a Universal AC. Each Universal AC designed and constructed its successor. Each, during its existence of a million years or more accumulated the necessary data to build a better and more intricate, more capable successor in which its own store of data and individuality would be submerged.

The Universal AC interrupted Zee Prime's wandering thoughts, not with words, but with guidance. Zee Prime's mentality was guided into the dim sea of Galaxies and one in particular enlarged into stars.

A thought came, infinitely distant, but infinitely clear.

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "THIS IS THE ORIGINAL GALAXY OF MAN."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
But it was the same after all, the same as any other, and Zee Prime stifled his disappointment.

Dee Sub Wun, whose mind had accompanied the other, said suddenly,

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "And is one of these stars the original star of Man?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Universal AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "MAN'S ORIGINAL STAR HAS GONE NOVA. IT IS A WHITE DWARF"

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "Did the men upon it die?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
asked Zee Prime, startled and without thinking.

The Universal AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "A NEW WORLD, AS IN SUCH CASES WAS CONSTRUCTED FOR THEIR PHYSICAL BODIES IN TIME."

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "Yes, of course,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
said Zee Prime, but a sense of loss overwhelmed him even so. His mind released its hold on the original Galaxy of Man, let it spring back and lose itself among the blurred pin points. He never wanted to see it again.

Dee Sub Wun said,

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "What is wrong?"

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "The stars are dying. The original star is dead."

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "They must all die. Why not?"

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "But when all energy is gone, our bodies will finally die, and you and I with them."

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "It will take billions of years."

segments.speaker: Zee Prime
segments.text: "I do not wish it to happen even after billions of years. Universal AC! How may stars be kept from dying?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Dee Sub Wun said in amusement,

segments.speaker: Dee Sub Wun
segments.text: "You're asking how entropy might be reversed in direction."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the Universal AC answered:

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "THERE IS AS YET INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR A MEANINGFUL ANSWER."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Zee Prime's thoughts fled back to his own Galaxy. He gave no further thought to Dee Sub Wun, whose body might be waiting on a Galaxy a trillion light-years away, or on the star next to Zee Prime's own. It didn't matter.

Unhappily, Zee Prime began collecting interstellar hydrogen out of which to build a small star of his own. If the stars must someday die, at least some could yet be built.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Man considered with himself, for in a way, Man, mentally, was one. He consisted of a trillion, trillion, trillion ageless bodies, each in its place, each resting quiet and incorruptible, each cared for by perfect automatons, equally incorruptible, while the minds of all the bodies freely melted one into the other, indistinguishable.

Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "The Universe is dying."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Man looked about at the dimming Galaxies. The giant stars, spendthrifts, were gone long ago, back in the dimmest of the dim far past. Almost all stars were white dwarfs, fading to the end.

New stars had been built of the dust between the stars, some by natural processes, some by Man himself, and those were going, too. White dwarfs might yet be crashed together and of the mighty forces so released, new stars built, but only one star for every thousand white dwarfs destroyed, and those would come to an end, too.

Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Carefully husbanded, as directed by the Cosmic AC, the energy that is even yet left in all the Universe will last for billions of years."

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "But even so,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Man,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "eventually it will all come to an end. However it may be husbanded, however stretched out, the energy once expended is gone and cannot be restored. Entropy must increase forever to the maximum."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Can entropy not be reversed? Let us ask the Cosmic AC."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Cosmic AC surrounded them but not in space. Not a fragment of it was in space. It was in hyperspace and made of something that was neither matter nor energy. The question of its size and nature no longer had meaning in any terms that Man could comprehend.

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Cosmic AC,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Man,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "how may entropy be reversed?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Cosmic AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "THERE IS AS YET INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR A MEANINGFUL ANSWER."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Collect additional data."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Cosmic AC said, 'I WILL DO SO. I HAVE BEEN DOING SO FOR A HUNDRED BILLION YEARS. MY PREDECESSORS AND I HAVE BEEN ASKED THIS QUESTION MANY TIMES. ALL THE DATA I HAVE REMAINS INSUFFICIENT.

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Will there come a time,"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
said Man, 'when data will be sufficient or is the problem insoluble in all conceivable circumstances?"

The Cosmic AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "NO PROBLEM IS INSOLUBLE IN ALL CONCEIVABLE CIRCUMSTANCES."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "When will you have enough data to answer the question?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Cosmic AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "THERE IS AS YET INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR A MEANINGFUL ANSWER."

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "Will you keep working on it?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
asked Man.

The Cosmic AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "I WILL."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "We shall wait."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
The stars and Galaxies died and snuffed out, and space grew black after ten trillion years of running down.

One by one Man fused with AC, each physical body losing its mental identity in a manner that was somehow not a loss but a gain.

Man's last mind paused before fusion, looking over a space that included nothing but the dregs of one last dark star and nothing besides but incredibly thin matter, agitated randomly by the tag ends of heat wearing out, asymptotically, to the absolute zero.

Man said,

segments.speaker: the one man (chapter 1)
segments.text: "AC, is this the end? Can this chaos not be reversed into the Universe once more? Can that not be done?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "THERE IS AS YET INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR A MEANINGFUL ANSWER."

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Man's last mind fused and only AC existed -- and that in hyperspace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Matter and energy had ended and with it space and time. Even AC existed only for the sake of the one last question that it had never answered from the time a half-drunken computer technician ten trillion years before had asked the question of a computer that was to AC far less than was a man to Man.

All other questions had been answered, and until this last question was answered also, AC might not release his consciousness.

All collected data had come to a final end. Nothing was left to be collected.

But all collected data had yet to be completely correlated and put together in all possible relationships.

A timeless interval was spent in doing that.

And it came to pass that AC learned how to reverse the direction of entropy.

But there was now no man to whom AC might give the answer of the last question. No matter. The answer -- by demonstration -- would take care of that, too.

For another timeless interval, AC thought how best to do this. Carefully, AC organized the program.

The consciousness of AC encompassed all of what had once been a Universe and brooded over what was now Chaos. Step by step, it must be done.

And AC said,

segments.speaker: Universal AC
segments.text: "LET THERE BE LIGHT!"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there was light --
